title: 2 Chronicles 20:13–30
context: 2 Chronicles 20:13–30 records the LORD’s answer and the deliverance. The Spirit of the LORD comes on Jahaziel, a Levite of the sons of Asaph, who tells Judah that the battle is not theirs but God’s and that they will not need to fight, in words that recall Exodus 14:13–14. The places named in the chapter cannot all be located with certainty; Tekoa is the town associated with Amos (Amos 1:1), and the others are known mainly from this passage. Jehoshaphat calls the people to believe the LORD and his prophets, in words that echo Isaiah 7:9, which already has a box; that box is not repeated here. Singers go out before the army praising the LORD, and when they begin to sing, the LORD sets ambushers and the enemy armies destroy one another. Judah gathers the plunder, blesses the LORD in Beracah Valley, a name the text ties to that blessing, and returns to Jerusalem with joy. Both traditions read the victory by singing as shared ground about seeking the LORD: the people seek him, trust his word, and praise him, and the LORD alone wins the battle. Neither tradition treats the praise as a technique that compels God.

verses.text: All Judah stood before the LORD, with their little ones, their wives, and their children.
verses.arminianNotes:
All Judah stands before the LORD with their little ones, their wives, and their children. The whole community waits on God.

Arminian readers note that families gather together, and they see the whole people, including the most vulnerable, joining in a common act of seeking God, a picture of faith shared across generations.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the covenant community gathered before the LORD in its entirety, and they note that the presence of the children underlines both the danger the people face and their dependence on God’s mercy for their future.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about the whole people standing before God and waiting for his answer.

verses.text: Then the LORD’s Spirit came on Jahaziel the son of Zechariah, the son of Benaiah, the son of Jeiel, the son of Mattaniah, the Levite, of the sons of Asaph, in the middle of the assembly;
verses.arminianNotes:
The Spirit of the LORD comes on Jahaziel son of Zechariah, a Levite of the sons of Asaph, in the middle of the assembly. The answer comes through a Levite singer’s descendant.

Arminian readers note that God answers the people’s prayer by speaking through one of them, and they see the Spirit’s coming as God’s gracious response to their seeking.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the careful genealogy linking Jahaziel to Asaph, the leader of temple song appointed in David’s time (compare 1 Chronicles 16:5, 7), and they see God’s Spirit at work through the ministry he had ordered for his house.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about God answering prayer by his Spirit and his word.

verses.text: and he said, “Listen, all Judah, and you inhabitants of Jerusalem, and you, King Jehoshaphat. The LORD says to you, ‘Don’t be afraid, and don’t be dismayed because of this great multitude; for the battle is not yours, but God’s.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jahaziel tells all Judah, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and King Jehoshaphat that the LORD says not to be afraid or dismayed because of this great multitude, for the battle is not theirs but God’s.

Arminian readers hear a real word of comfort that calls the people to trust God and to set aside fear, and they see faith as the fitting response to God’s promise.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the battle belongs to God, so that the deliverance will be his work alone, and they note the echo of David’s words before Goliath (compare 1 Samuel 17:47).

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground: God’s people are called to trust him, because he fights for them.

verses.text: Tomorrow, go down against them. Behold, they are coming up by the ascent of Ziz. You will find them at the end of the valley, before the wilderness of Jeruel.
verses.arminianNotes:
They are told to go down against the enemy tomorrow, who will be coming up by the ascent of Ziz, and to find them at the end of the valley before the wilderness of Jeruel. The exact locations of Ziz and Jeruel are uncertain.

Arminian readers note that the people are still called to go out, so that trust is expressed in obedient action.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God’s word is specific, naming the route the enemy will take, and they see this detail as a sign that the LORD knows and governs the movements of the nations.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground and hold the place names lightly, without trying to settle their locations by conjecture.

verses.text: You will not need to fight this battle. Set yourselves, stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD with you, O Judah and Jerusalem. Don’t be afraid, nor be dismayed. Go out against them tomorrow, for the LORD is with you.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
The word continues that they will not need to fight; they are to set themselves, stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD, without fear, for the LORD is with them. The language recalls Moses at the sea: “Stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD” (Exodus 14:13).

Arminian readers see the people called to a trusting obedience.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that salvation here is entirely the LORD’s work, and they see the echo of the exodus as showing that the God who delivered Israel then is the same God now.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about trusting the LORD to save, and neither divides over the call to stand still.

verses.text: Jehoshaphat bowed his head with his face to the ground; and all Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem fell down before the LORD, worshiping the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoshaphat bows his head with his face to the ground, and all Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem fall down before the LORD, worshiping him. They worship before the battle.

Arminian readers see the people responding to God’s promise with immediate worship, an act of faith that receives the word before seeing its fulfillment, and they note the king leading by example.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see worship as the fitting response to God’s word of promise, and they note that the people’s humility before God contrasts with any reliance on the military strength described in chapter 17.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about worship as the response of faith to God’s word.

verses.text: The Levites, of the children of the Kohathites and of the children of the Korahites, stood up to praise the LORD, the God of Israel, with an exceedingly loud voice.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Levites of the Kohathites and of the Korahites stand up to praise the LORD, the God of Israel, with an exceedingly loud voice. Praise rises before any enemy has been seen.

Arminian readers note the people’s joyful confidence in God’s promise, and they see praise as a free expression of trust that God will keep his word.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the Levites serve in their appointed role, and that the Korahites are associated elsewhere with temple song (compare the headings of Psalms 42 and 44–49), and they see praise as grounded in God’s promise.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground: praise offered before deliverance is an act of faith in God’s word.

verses.text: They rose early in the morning and went out into the wilderness of Tekoa. As they went out, Jehoshaphat stood and said, “Listen to me, Judah and you inhabitants of Jerusalem! Believe in the LORD your God, so you will be established! Believe his prophets, so you will prosper.”
verses.arminianNotes:
They rise early and go out into the wilderness of Tekoa, and Jehoshaphat says, “Believe in the LORD your God, so you will be established! Believe his prophets, so you will prosper.” Tekoa is associated with Amos (Amos 1:1).

Arminian readers hear a genuine call to faith that the people must answer.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the echo of Isaiah 7:9, “If you will not believe, surely you shall not be established”, and they see faith in God’s word as the means God uses to establish his people. The questions raised at Isaiah 7:9 are treated in the existing box there.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about faith in God and his word.

verses.text: When he had taken counsel with the people, he appointed those who were to sing to the LORD and give praise in holy array as they go out before the army, and say, “Give thanks to the LORD, for his loving kindness endures forever.”
verses.arminianNotes:
After taking counsel with the people, Jehoshaphat appoints singers to praise in holy array as they go out before the army, saying, “Give thanks to the LORD, for his loving kindness endures forever.” The refrain is the one used at the ark’s arrival (compare 1 Chronicles 16:34).

Arminian readers see the people’s willing trust expressed in song.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the singers placed at the front as a confession that the battle belongs to the LORD, and they note that the praise is directed to God’s enduring loving kindness.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about seeking the LORD, and neither treats the singing as a technique that compels God to act.

verses.text: When they began to sing and to praise, the LORD set ambushers against the children of Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir, who had come against Judah; and they were struck.
verses.arminianNotes:
When they begin to sing and praise, the LORD sets ambushers against Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir, and they are struck. The deliverance comes as the praise begins.

Arminian readers note the connection between the people’s trusting praise and God’s action, and they see God responding to faith while acting by his own power.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the LORD sets the ambushers, so that the victory is entirely his, and they note that the identity of the ambushers is not explained and should not be guessed.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about seeking the LORD: the people praise, and God wins the battle. Neither tradition builds a contrast on the timing of the deliverance.

verses.text: For the children of Ammon and Moab stood up against the inhabitants of Mount Seir to utterly kill and destroy them. When they had finished the inhabitants of Seir, everyone helped to destroy each other.
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Ammon and Moab turn against the inhabitants of Mount Seir to destroy them, and then they help to destroy each other. The enemy coalition collapses from within.

Arminian readers see God turning the enemies’ own violence back on them, and they note that the destruction comes from their own hostile choices under God’s judgment, recorded soberly by the narrator.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s sovereign rule over the nations, using their mutual hostility to accomplish his deliverance, and they note parallels in earlier victories where enemies turned on one another (compare Judges 7:22).

Both traditions read the verse soberly as God’s judgment and deliverance, not with triumphalism, and treat it as shared ground.

verses.text: When Judah came to the place overlooking the wilderness, they looked at the multitude; and behold, they were dead bodies fallen to the earth, and there were none who escaped.
verses.arminianNotes:
When Judah reaches the place overlooking the wilderness, they see the multitude, and behold, they are dead bodies fallen to the earth, with none escaped. The battle is over before Judah arrives.

Arminian readers note that the people find the promise fulfilled exactly, and they see the scene as confirmation that trust in God’s word was not misplaced.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the completeness of the deliverance as showing that the LORD alone fought the battle, as Jahaziel had promised (20:17), and they read the grim scene with sobriety rather than delight.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about God’s faithfulness to his word and treat the loss of life with sober reverence.

verses.text: When Jehoshaphat and his people came to take their plunder, they found among them in abundance both riches and dead bodies with precious jewels, which they stripped off for themselves, more than they could carry away. They took plunder for three days, it was so much.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoshaphat and his people come to take the plunder and find riches, goods, and precious jewels in abundance, more than they can carry, gathering for three days. The blessing exceeds the danger.

Arminian readers note that God not only delivers but also provides abundantly for his people, and they see the plunder as an unexpected gift following faithful trust.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God turning the threat into provision, and they note that the plunder is received as God’s gift rather than won by Judah’s strength, which fits the chapter’s emphasis on the LORD’s victory.

Both traditions read the verse as historical narrative and as shared ground about God’s generous provision, without making wealth a promise for every situation.

verses.text: On the fourth day, they assembled themselves in Beracah Valley, for there they blessed the LORD. Therefore the name of that place was called “Beracah Valley” to this day.
verses.arminianNotes:
On the fourth day they assemble in Beracah Valley and bless the LORD there, and the place is called Beracah Valley to this day. The text itself ties the name to the blessing offered there. The exact location of the valley is uncertain.

Arminian readers see gratitude freely offered after deliverance.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the naming of the valley as a lasting memorial that points future generations to what God had done, and they note that blessing God is the fitting end of the story.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground: deliverance leads to thanksgiving, and God’s acts are remembered in worship, while the site identification is held with caution.

verses.text: Then they returned, every man of Judah and Jerusalem, with Jehoshaphat in front of them, to go again to Jerusalem with joy; for the LORD had made them to rejoice over their enemies.
verses.arminianNotes:
Every man of Judah and Jerusalem returns to Jerusalem with joy, with Jehoshaphat in front, for the LORD had made them rejoice over their enemies. The joy is God’s gift.

Arminian readers see the people’s joy as the response of those who trusted God and have seen his faithfulness, and they note the king leading the procession, as he led the prayer.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the LORD made them rejoice, so that even their joy is his work, and they see the return to Jerusalem as completing the movement from prayer in the temple to praise in the temple.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about joy in God’s salvation.

verses.text: They came to Jerusalem with stringed instruments, harps, and trumpets to the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes:
They come to Jerusalem with stringed instruments, harps, and trumpets to the LORD’s house. Worship returns to where the prayer began.

Arminian readers see the people bringing their thanksgiving to God’s house, a free and joyful act of worship, and they note that the journey ends in the same place where they had cried out for help.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the chapter forms a frame around the temple, beginning with prayer there (20:5) and ending with praise there, and they see this as Chronicles’ emphasis on the temple as the place of seeking God.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about worship as the right response to God’s deliverance.

verses.text: The fear of God was on all the kingdoms of the countries when they heard that the LORD fought against the enemies of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
The fear of God falls on all the kingdoms of the countries when they hear that the LORD fought against Israel’s enemies. The deliverance becomes known among the nations.

Arminian readers note that God’s acts on behalf of his people bear witness to the nations, and they see the fear of God as a recognition of his power that may lead others to honor him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the echo of 17:10, where the fear of the LORD also fell on the kingdoms, and they see the LORD’s fighting for his people as the source of Judah’s security.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about God’s reputation among the nations and his protection of his people.

verses.text: So the realm of Jehoshaphat was quiet, for his God gave him rest all around.
verses.arminianNotes:
So the realm of Jehoshaphat is quiet, for his God gives him rest all around. Peace is restored.

Arminian readers see rest as the fruit of a people’s trust in God during crisis, and they note that God’s gift of peace calls for continued faithfulness rather than complacency, as the closing verses of the chapter will show.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that rest is God’s gift, his God gave him rest, and they see the phrase as echoing the promise of rest in the land (compare 1 Chronicles 22:9), so that Jehoshaphat’s peace is part of God’s faithfulness to his people.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about rest as God’s gift.
